title: Reduction
description: A way to solve problem `from` with an algorithm for problem `to`, run on an instance built from the input graph. It turns an algorithm for `to` into one for `from`, and a lower bound for `from` into one for `to`.

title.description: Short name of the technique, e.g. 'Line graph'.

to.description: The problem whose algorithm is used.

randomness.description: Set to 'randomized' if the reduction itself uses randomness (e.g. shattering): results derived with it are randomized even if the algorithm for `to` is deterministic.

instance.description: The graph the algorithm for `to` runs on, with its parameters in terms of n and Delta of the input graph.

graph.description: same: the input graph G; line-graph: L(G); clique-product: G x K_{Delta+1}; components: the connected components of a subgraph of G that remain after a first phase (e.g. shattering).

graph_class.description: Only for reductions that work on one graph class, e.g. 3-coloring an oriented cycle from an MIS. Left out for reductions that work on all graphs.

runtime.description: Total rounds for `from`. T is the runtime of the algorithm for `to` on the instance; the output parameters of `to` are c (colors of a coloring) and C, D (colors and cluster diameter of a network decomposition).

models.description: Models in which the reduction has this runtime.

year.description: Year of the earliest publication, if the reduction is attributed to a paper.

sources.description: Papers the reduction is attributed to; left out for folklore.

url.description: Link to the referenced theorem, e.g. in the HTML version on arXiv (see scripts/link_theorems.py).

comments.description: Short note, not a full sentence. [[result-id]] links a result, [[paper-id]] a paper.

colors.description: Number of colors, for coloring problems, in terms of the input graph.

expr.description: Machine-readable form, as for results, with the additional variables T, c, C, D and the operator -. Example: 'T + O(C * D)'.
